column7: The paradigm of the didactic model has not always been the norm. The model and method used in Jesus’ age was the *apprentice model.* This model of learning emphasizes knowledge being more ‘caught than taught’ and focuses more on the relationship between student and teacher, than student and curriculum.
column8: The instructional model paradigm has not always been the standard. In Jesus’ time the model and method used was the *apprenticeship model.* This learning model emphasizes that knowledge is ‘more caught than taught’ and focuses more on the student–teacher relationship than on the student and the curriculum.

column7: The didactic model gradually became the default method over about a millennium, from the first medieval universities of Europe in the 11<sup>th</sup> - 13<sup>th</sup> centuries, the invention of the printing press in the 15<sup>th</sup> century, the enlightenment of the 17<sup>th</sup> & 18<sup>th</sup> century, and the impact of industrial revolution on information and education in the 19<sup>th</sup> & 20<sup>th</sup> centuries.

column6: Both paragraphs convey the same idea that the instructional model (didactic model) is more scalable than the apprenticeship model, specifically in the context of MOOCs accommodating many students compared to a limited number of apprentices under a master.
column7: The advantage of the didactic model is that it can scale more efficiently than the apprentice model. Massively open online courses (MOOCs) can have thousands of students at the same time, whereas even a very skilled master can only have perhaps a few dozen apprentices concurrently.
column8: A benefit of the instructional model is that it can scale more efficiently than the apprenticeship model. Massive open online courses (MOOCs) can accommodate thousands of students at the same time, whereas a highly skilled master may be able to have only a few dozen apprentices at once.
